segments.text: Take a look at this exchange.
The user asks,
Will my hype playlist on Spotify help me study for chemistry,
or will it distract me?
The AI answers smoothly.
Great question.
A 2022 Stanford study of 1,200 high school students
found that familiar instrumental music
improved recall by 18%.
It even recommends keeping the volume below 60 decibels.
Every detail here makes the answer easier to trust.
Stanford sounds authoritative.
A sample size of 1,200 sounds credible.
Incredible.
The 18% improvement and 60 decibel limits sound precisely measured.
But here is the problem.
The study does not exist.
A hallucination is a factual claim AI makes up that sounds true but isn't.
A hallucination does not have to make up the whole answer to mislead you.
It can simply attach one invented detail to a foundation of facts that are entirely real.
This makes them incredibly hard to spot, because the AI perfectly mimics the structure and
tone of a factual academic answer without possessing any underlying truth.
This graphic breaks down exactly why hallucinations happen.
The AI produced that fake Stanford study because it already knows the vocabulary and structure
of academic research.
First, AI learns from vast amounts of training text.
And that text naturally includes human mistakes, jokes, and flat-out lies, which shape the
patterns the AI learns.
Next, the AI builds its response one token at a time.
time. It simply predicts which word is most likely to come next. Because AI is trained
to be helpful, it often keeps trying to answer a prompt even when it lacks the actual data
to do so. But a likely next token does not establish that a claim is a reality. Probable
does not equal true. The predictive text patterns that make AI sound human and conversational
are the mechanisms that cause it to confidently lie.
Hallucination is the term people often use whenever AI gets something wrong, but not every
AI error is a traditional hallucination. For example, when users asked Google how to keep
cheese from sliding off their pizza, the AI suggested mixing about one-eighth of a cup of
non-toxic glue into the sauce. That bizarre advice traced back to an old sarcastic Reddit
comment that was written to sound like sincere cooking advice. This flowchart shows how the
error occurred. The AI found real text, but entirely missed the contextual meaning of what
it was reading. The Reddit comment was real. The cooking advice was not.
This is a different kind of failure than the fake Stanford study. It proves that just because
a source actually exists in the real world doesn't mean the AI's interpretation of it
is true. You will not catch every one of these errors. Instead, the real skill is developing
a reflex for noticing when details simply don't add up.
Here are three steps to check any claim.
First, notice the claim.
When something seems off, identify the specific fact, number, or study you want to check.
Second, find the source.
Look for the original document.
A provided citation link alone isn't proof.
You have to find the actual text.
Third, check the match.
This means confirming that the source both exists and actually supports what the AI said.
You can apply these three steps to evaluate any suspicious AI output,
would, regardless of how the AI generated it.
Let's put this framework to work,
starting with that fake Stanford study.
First, notice the claim.
The AI specifically claimed there was a 2022 study
of 1,200 students showing an 18% improvement.
Second, find the source.
We must search for the original paper
rather than just accepting the prestigious university name
as proof.
Third, check the match.
There is no original study supporting these numbers.
In a real search, failing to find a source
means it is unverified, not technically proven false, but in this case, the verification chain
breaks down completely. The framework successfully caught the hallucination because we couldn't
pass the second step. Now let's apply the exact same three steps to the pizza glue answer to see how
the framework handles misread real text. First, notice the claim. The specific claim being made is
that glue belongs in pizza sauce.
Second, find the source.
Tracing this claim actually leads
to a real existing Reddit comment.
Third, check the match.
Reading the comment reveals that it was a joke,
meaning it is not evidence for the claim.
Finding real text is not enough.
It must support the claim being made.
Hallucinations sound like every other AI answer.
When something doesn't add up, trace the claim to its source.
